title: Warming up, embouchure and breaking in valves
summary: He compares warming up to a pitcher and explains why Bix broke in the valve springs.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Now I know that this is old hat to you but I do think that people will read what we're saying here today or listen to what we're saying here today who may not know anything about the techniques of blowing such a horn.

Now I think it might be well for us to say something about how you go about determining what is a good horn or/one horn is better than the other. And what you do with these valves when you say breaking them in. It's obviously a matter of loosening them up in some way. But I would rather have you talk about it in your professional way. (LAUGHTER).
Having never had a cornet to my lips. (LAUGHTER).

Well when I blew that 'Blue Bells of Scotland' I hadn't warmed up enough. Your lips have to get loose, you have to loosen them up. I compare it to warming up on the horn, to a baseball pitcher before a game. He gets out there and he throws easy at first and his muscles get looser and he gets the muscles used to throwing and his muscles loosen up. Well the same thing comparably with the

embouchure (umbrella?) or your lips. And the muscles surrounding the lips or around the lips, not just the lips itself. There are a lot of muscles go all over your face. And these muscles if you warm up properly and blow correctly from your diaphragm and get the mouthpiece in the correct position and blow, why they'll loosen up after, oh, it takes, it takes me longer now to loosen up. Because I guess my muscles are getting a little older naturally. (LAUGHTER).
You're a little heavier and your wind is a little shorter, huh? (LAUGHTER).
That's right. No, the wind's alright. But the comparison in blowing coronet or trumpet, they're the same or any trombone or any instrument like that. You must warm up before you play.
Well what about breaking in the instrument that you were just talking about, as you were just talking about it rather?
Well it's actually a valve deal. Pressing the valves down a certain way, the correct way. And Bix wanted to blow the horn anyway really you know. (LAUGHTER).
Yes. And it was nice of him you know, I mean.
But doesn't it have something to do with the flexibility of the ...
Yes, because in jazz when you have to make notes that hardly can be written down, it would seem to me...
Well that's a different thing, I mean it's a different thing. It's just a matter of how you press the valves down you know.
But they would have to be quite loose for you to make those .....

Oh they certainly do and those springs have to be functioning. There has to be a certain tension and that's what he wanted to do really was to get the tension on the valves, of the springs, I mean the springs is what I mean to say, the springs on the valves a certain tension so that they come up fast. If they come up too slow it's no good. You be inbetween and you get a bad sound. But that's what he wanted to do. And that's what he did really. And as far as, oh, I must tell you
